**Famous American Composers (Classical & Contemporary)**  
*(Note: “Most famous” is inherently subjective; the following list highlights composers who have had a lasting impact on American music, achieved widespread recognition, and whose works are frequently performed, recorded, or studied.)*

| Composer | Lifespan | Key Contributions / Notable Works | Why They’re Famous |
|----------|----------|-----------------------------------|--------------------|
| **George Gershwin** (1898–1937) | *Rhapsody in Blue* (1924), *An American in Paris* (1928), *Porgy and Bess* (1935) | Blended jazz idioms with classical forms; created one‑hour operas and symphonic poems that remain staples of the repertoire. | His music bridged Broadway, jazz, and concert hall audiences; *Rhapsody in Blue* is an iconic American soundscape. |
| **Aaron Copland** (1900–1990) | *Appalachian Spring* (1944), *Elmer Gantry* (1947), *Fanfare for the Common Man* (1942) | Developed a distinctly “American” orchestral style—open harmonies, folk melodies, and expansive textures. | His works epitomize mid‑20th‑century American optimism; *Fanfare for the Common Man* is instantly recognizable. |
| **Leonard Bernstein** (1918–1990) | *West Side Story* (1957), *Candide* (1959), *On the Town* (1944) | A conductor, pianist, and composer who brought Broadway and classical worlds together; his conducting of the New York Philharmonic made him a household name. | He popularized classical music through television concerts and his charismatic teaching; *West Side Story* remains a cultural touchstone. |
| **Samuel Barber** (1910–1981) | *Adagio for Strings* (1936), *Violin Concerto* (1939), *Knoxville: Summer of 1915* (1944) | Known for lyrical, emotionally direct music; his *Adagio* has become a go‑to piece for solemn occasions worldwide. | His music is widely performed and recorded; he won the Pulitzer Prize for Music twice. |
| **Charles Ives** (1874–1954) | *The Unanswered Question* (1908), *Concord Sonata* (1906) | Pioneered experimental techniques—polytonality, polyrhythms—and incorporated American folk tunes into art music. | Considered a precursor to modernist American composers; his work influenced later generations. |
| **William Grant Still** (1895–1978) | *Afro-American Symphony* (1930), *Bluebird* (1935) | First African‑American composer to have a symphony performed by a major orchestra; blended blues, jazz, and classical idioms. | He broke racial barriers in classical music and inspired future Black composers. |
| **Philip Glass** (born 1937) | *Einstein on the Beach* (1976), *Glassworks* (1982), *Koyaanisqatsi* (1983) | Minimalist composer known for repetitive structures, phase shifting, and collaborations with visual media. | His music permeates film, theater, and popular culture; he’s a leading figure in late‑20th‑century minimalism. |
| **Steve Reich** (born 1936) | *Music for 18 Musicians* (1976), *Different Trains* (1988) | Pioneer of phasing patterns and tape loops; his works explore rhythm, process, and social themes. | He helped bring minimalism to mainstream audiences; his pieces are staples of contemporary orchestras. |
| **John Adams** (born 1947) | *Nixon in China* (1987), *Short Ride in a Fast Machine* (1992), *The Death of Klinghoffer* (1991) | Combines minimalism with lush orchestration; his operas tackle historical and political subjects. | He’s a Pulitzer‑winning composer whose works are regularly staged worldwide. |
| **John Williams** (born 1932) | *Star Wars*, *Indiana Jones*, *Jurassic Park*, *Harry Potter* (film scores) | One of the most prolific film composers; his leitmotifs and thematic development are textbook examples of cinematic scoring. | His music is instantly recognizable; he’s earned multiple Oscars and Grammys. |
| **John Corigliano** (born 1945) | *The Ghosts of Versailles* (1991), *The Red Violin* (1998) | Pulitzer‑winning composer known for lyrical yet complex orchestral writing. | He’s a respected educator and composer whose works are frequently performed. |
| **John Cage** (1912–1992) | *4′33″* (1952), *Sonatas and Interludes* (1940) | Experimental composer who challenged notions of what constitutes music; introduced prepared piano and indeterminacy. | His ideas reshaped contemporary composition and performance practice. |
| **John Rutter** (born 1945) | *Requiem* (1985), *The Lord's Prayer* (1990) | Though British‑born, he’s been active in the U.S.; known for choral works that blend traditional tonality with modern harmonies. | His choral music is widely performed by choirs across America. |

---

### How to Explore Their Music

1. **Listen to Recordings** – Many of these composers have landmark recordings available on streaming platforms (Spotify, Apple Music, Tidal).  
2. **Attend Live Performances** – Check local symphonies, opera houses, and chamber ensembles; many programs feature works by these composers.  
3. **Read Scores** – If you play an instrument or study music theory, look at the scores to see how they structure harmony, rhythm, and orchestration.  
4. **Watch Documentaries/Interviews** – Biographical documentaries (e.g., *The Life of John Williams*, *Philip Glass: The Glass Family*) offer insight into their creative processes.  

---

### Quick Reference Links

| Composer | Official Website / Archive | Notable Recordings |
|----------|---------------------------|--------------------|
| George Gershwin | [Gershwin Foundation](https://www.gershwin.org/) | *Rhapsody in Blue* (Orchestral Society of New York) |
| Aaron Copland | [Copland House](http://www.coplandhouse.org/) | *Appalachian Spring* (Boston Symphony Orchestra) |
| Leonard Bernstein | [Bernstein Center](https://bernsteincenter.org/) | *West Side Story* (NY Philharmonic) |
| Samuel Barber | [Barber Foundation](https://barberfoundation.org/) | *Adagio for Strings* (Chicago Symphony) |
| Charles Ives | [Ives Institute](https://www.ivesinstitute.org/) | *Concord Sonata* (New York Philharmonic) |
| William Grant Still | [Still Foundation](https://stillfoundation.org/) | *Afro‑American Symphony* (Philadelphia Orchestra) |
| Philip Glass | [Glassworks](https://glassworks.com/) | *Glassworks* (London Symphony Orchestra) |
| Steve Reich | [Steve Reich Ensemble](https://stevereichensemble.org/) | *Music for 18 Musicians* (Berlin Philharmonic) |
| John Adams | [John Adams Official](https://johnadams.com/) | *Nixon in China* (NY Philharmonic) |
| John Williams | [John Williams Official](https://johnwilliams.com/) | *Star Wars* (Hollywood Studio Symphony) |
| John Corigliano | [Corigliano Official](https://corigliano.com/) | *The Ghosts of Versailles* (NY Philharmonic) |
| John Cage | [Cage Archive](https://cagearchive.org/) | *Sonatas and Interludes* (Boston Symphony) |
| John Rutter | [Rutter Official](https://www.johnrutter.com/) | *Requiem* (London Symphony Orchestra) |

Feel free to dive deeper into any of these composers—each offers a unique window into the evolution of American music.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "Who was the most famous composers in United States." They want a list of famous composers in the US. We should provide a list of notable American composers. Provide some context. Probably mention classical and popular? The question is ambiguous: "most famous composers" could refer to classical composers or all composers. We'll interpret as classical composers. Provide a list: George Gershwin, Aaron Copland, Leonard Bernstein, John Williams (film composer), Philip Glass, Steve Reich, Samuel Barber, Charles Ives, William Grant Still, John Adams, etc. Also mention contemporary like Hans Zimmer? But he's German-born but works in US. Provide a short description.

We can also mention that "most famous" is subjective. Provide a list sorted by influence/popularity. Provide brief bios. Provide references. Use bullet points. Provide a short introduction.
